name: The Learning Trap
title: The Learning Trap
answer: The Learning Trap is the risk that AI removes the struggle learning requires, so the assignment gets finished while the learning does not happen, and often no one notices, including the student. It matters because the loss is invisible: a student can look successful while building nothing that lasts.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The Learning Trap is the quiet risk that students skip the thinking that learning depends on, rather than the louder worry about cheating. Knowledge that lasts is built when a student wrestles with a math problem, drafts a paragraph three times, or works to explain an idea in her own words. An AI tool can remove that struggle in seconds. The work then gets done while the learning does not. What makes the trap hard to catch is that it can happen without anyone noticing, including the student herself.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Schools can design around much of this trap with the five moves shown in Figure 1.5, which recur throughout the book and require no special software. What they require is that the assignment be built so the student has to think. For younger children the text gives a simpler answer: in the early grades, most AI use should sit with the teacher, who uses it to plan and prepare, not with the child. Beyond that early grades guidance, the text does not set out separate practice for each grade band, though the German study it cites covers grades 1 through 12.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book points to two studies. The Turkish math study showed practice scores going up while real learning went down, and students could not tell the difference. A German platform gave AI feedback on writing to more than 14,000 students in grades 1 through 12, and nearly half of them, 48 percent, did not change a single character of their work after reading the feedback, a rate that barely moved from first grade to twelfth (Jansen et al., 2025). The book's conclusion from this is that feedback nobody acts on teaches nothing, however good it is.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits the text sets are about what schools and teachers must decide, not what a tool can decide for them. The risk is skipped thinking that goes unnoticed, and the student cannot be relied on to detect it, so the responsibility for noticing sits with adults. The design decisions stay human: how an assignment is built so that a student has to think, and where AI sits in the early grades, which the text places with the teacher for planning and preparation rather than with the child. Because none of the five moves needs special software, these remain choices of practice rather than purchases.
